readerTitle: Tropicana changed one carton and lost its customers' eyes
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Tropicana, 2009년 포장 리디자인) + 가상 적용 (예산 관리 앱)
insight: 포장과 로고는 장식이 아니라 고객이 몇 초 만에 우리를 찾아내는 길잡이다. 이것을 바꾸면 고객은 우리를 다시 찾아야 한다.
misconception: 더 현대적이고 깔끔한 디자인이면 고객도 더 좋아할 것이다. 낡아 보이는 포장은 바꿀수록 이득이다.

sources.text: Stuart Elliott, "Tropicana Discovers Some Buyers Are Passionate About Packaging," The New York Times, February 2009 (새 디자인 요소, 고객 항의, 이전 포장 복귀 발표)
Advertising Age, April 2009, Tropicana Pure Premium 리디자인 이후 매출 감소 보도 (소매 판매 데이터 인용)
Jenni Romaniuk, Building Distinctive Brand Assets (2018) — 독특한 브랜드 자산 개념

factChecks.note: 리디자인 출시 시점(2009년 1월)과 이전 포장 복귀 발표(2009년 2월, 약 두 달 이내)는 NYT 기사로 확인하세요.
새 디자인 요소(빨대 꽂힌 오렌지 이미지 삭제, 주스 잔 클로즈업, 세로 로고, 오렌지 모양 뚜껑)는 NYT 기사 기준입니다. 게시 전 다시 확인하세요.
"매출 약 20% 감소"는 Advertising Age가 소매 판매 데이터를 인용해 보도한 수치입니다. 1차 기사 제목·날짜·URL을 확인하세요. 카드에는 "reportedly"로 표기했고, 손실액·디자인 비용 등 다른 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.
"자체 브랜드(store brand)처럼 보였다"는 고객 반응은 당시 보도에 널리 나온 내용이지만 직접 인용은 쓰지 않았습니다. 회사 측 발언도 인용하지 않고 요지만 서술했습니다.

cards.title: Tropicana changed one carton and lost its customers' eyes
body: In January 2009, Tropicana Pure Premium orange juice arrived in US stores in a sleek new carton.
The juice inside was the same. Within about two months, the company announced it was bringing the old carton back.

image.label: An orange juice carton vanishing among similar cartons on a shelf
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 마트 냉장 진열대에 비슷한 흰색 주스 팩이 줄지어 있고, 그중 하나가 반투명하게 사라지는 모습. 실제 Tropicana 로고·상표·포장 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your carton looks dated.
body: It's 2008. You run a leading orange juice brand. For years the carton has shown an orange with a straw stuck in it. Your design agency calls it old-fashioned and proposes a clean, modern look.

options.text: Launch the full modern redesign to look fresh and premium
options.feedback: You gain a modern look, but you throw away the cues shoppers use to spot you. If they can't find you fast, they grab something else.

options.text: Refresh the details, but keep the orange-and-straw and logo, and test it on a real shelf
options.feedback: You look current without making loyal buyers search for you. Testing on a shelf shows whether people still find you in seconds.

options.text: Change nothing. The carton is working
options.feedback: Safe for now, and it protects recognition. But never updating can slowly make a brand feel tired.

cards.title: The new carton looked like everyone else's.
body: Tropicana chose a full redesign. The orange with the straw was gone, replaced by a close-up glass of juice. The logo turned sideways. The cap became a plastic orange.
Customers complained by letter, phone and email. Many said it looked like a cheap store brand. Some said they simply couldn't find it.
Sales of the line reportedly fell about 20% in under two months. In February 2009, the company announced the old carton was coming back.

image.label: Old carton with fruit image beside a plain new carton
image.brief: 두 개의 가상 주스 팩 비교. 왼쪽은 빨대 꽂힌 오렌지 그림이 크게 있는 팩, 오른쪽은 흰 바탕에 주스 잔만 있는 밋밋한 팩. 오른쪽 팩 옆에 물음표. 실제 로고·브랜드명 없이.

cards.title: Distinctive assets
body: **Distinctive assets** are the cues customers link to one brand: a picture, a color, a shape, a logo. They let people recognize you without reading or thinking.
The orange with a straw was one of these. Shoppers didn't study it. They spotted it from across the aisle and reached for it. The redesign removed the very thing that made the carton easy to find.

cards.title: Shoppers scan. They don't read.
body: In a busy aisle, people decide in seconds. They look for familiar shapes and colors, not words.
When the cue disappears, three things happen:
list: They **compare** with rivals they used to ignore
The new look sends a **different signal**, here "generic" instead of "the one I trust"
cards.callout: A modern design can be better looking and still worse at its main job: being found.

cards.title: This isn't a case against change.
body: Brands do update their look and survive. The safer path is usually gradual: refresh around the cues people know, and keep the core ones.

The hard part is that customers can't always tell you which cues matter. In a focus group they may praise a new design. On the shelf they act differently. Test changes in real buying conditions, and roll them out in steps you can undo.

cards.title: Now it's a budgeting app.
body: Your budgeting app has a bright green icon with a little piggy bank. Users mention the pig often. A new designer wants a flat purple icon with a simple letter mark to look more grown-up.

options.text: Switch to the purple letter icon in the next update
options.feedback: It may look sharper, but users find apps by icon color and shape on a crowded home screen. Some will think the app vanished or was replaced.

options.text: Keep green and the pig, modernize the drawing, and test with a share of users first
options.feedback: You get a cleaner look while keeping the cues people use to find you. A staged release shows problems before everyone sees them.

options.text: Ask users in a survey which icon they prefer
options.feedback: It gives a signal, but people judge designs differently on a survey than on their own home screen. Watch behavior too.

cards.title: Don't redesign away the way customers find you.
body: Before changing a logo, package or icon, ask what people use to recognize you in a few seconds, and keep it.
**Try it today:** show a friend your product, sign or website for two seconds. Ask what they remember. That is the asset to protect.
